title: Readiness, stalled rollouts and choosing settings
summary: Diagnose a stalled rollout from its evidence, understand what readiness means to the controller, and choose readiness and deadline settings for a simple web service.
prereqText: From the previous lesson: the ceiling (replicas + maxSurge) and floor (replicas − maxUnavailable available) that bound a rolling update.

blocks.html: It is Friday. You apply a new image and your pipeline prints "Waiting for rollout to finish: 1 out of 3 new replicas have been updated..." and keeps printing it. Nobody paged you; the site still works. Is the deploy broken, slow, or fine? The answer is in a few lines of evidence, and you are about to read them. (Pipeline message style as in the docs' rollout example; this specific scenario is invented.) [source]

blocks.instructions: The outputs below are invented, illustrative simulations written for this course, not from a real cluster. Open the evidence you think you need (you do not have to open all of it), then choose the best-supported conclusion.
blocks.debrief: You should have noticed that the Pods are Running but not ready, and that the old Pods are still serving. "Running" is a container state; readiness is a separate condition that the probe decides. The stalled rollout is the limits from the last lesson plus a readiness probe that never succeeds.

config.situation: Deployment web, 3 replicas, default RollingUpdate (25% / 25%), progressDeadlineSeconds 600. Ten minutes ago the image changed from v1 to v2.
config.question: Which conclusion is best supported by the evidence?
config.terminalLabel: Simulated output - illustrative, not from a real cluster

evidence.label: Check the ReplicaSets
evidence.content:
NAME            DESIRED  CURRENT  READY
web-6b4f8c9d    3        3        3
web-7d9c5a1e    1        1        0
evidence.reading: The old ReplicaSet still has 3 ready Pods; the new one has 1 Pod that is not ready. Total 4 is the ceiling for 3 replicas with 25% surge.

evidence.label: Check the Pods
evidence.content:
NAME                  READY  STATUS   RESTARTS
web-6b4f8c9d-aaaaa    1/1    Running  0
web-6b4f8c9d-bbbbb    1/1    Running  0
web-6b4f8c9d-ccccc    1/1    Running  0
web-7d9c5a1e-ddddd    0/1    Running  0
evidence.reading: The new Pod is Running, not crashing (0 restarts), but 0/1 ready.

evidence.label: Read the Pod events
evidence.content: Warning  Unhealthy  Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 500
evidence.reading: The readiness probe itself is failing, with the application answering 500.

evidence.label: Check the Deployment condition
evidence.reading: The controller reports that the rollout has not progressed within its deadline. It has not rolled back.

evidence.label: Check Pod restarts / image pull
evidence.content: Image pulled successfully; container started; restarts: 0
evidence.reading: Rules out an image pull error and a crash loop.

conclusions.label: The new version starts but fails its readiness probe, so the rollout is stuck at the surge ceiling while old Pods serve.
conclusions.explanation: Matches the ReplicaSet counts (ceiling reached), 0/1 ready, 0 restarts and a failing readiness probe with HTTP 500.

conclusions.label: The cluster is out of capacity, so the new Pod cannot be scheduled.
conclusions.explanation: The Pod is Running; a scheduling problem would show Pending.

conclusions.label: The image cannot be pulled.
conclusions.explanation: The image was pulled and the container started.

conclusions.label: The rollout is just slow; wait longer.
conclusions.explanation: The deadline has already passed and the probe returns 500, which is not a transient wait. Waiting will not fix a failing probe.

assumptions: Invented outputs, formatted like typical kubectl output but not produced by one.
Application behaviour (HTTP 500) is an illustrative bug.

blocks.title: What readiness is, and how it drives rollouts
blocks.html:
A readiness probe tells Kubernetes when a container is ready to accept traffic. [source] While it fails, the kubelet marks the Pod not ready (it keeps the container running and keeps probing), and the EndpointSlice controller removes the Pod's IP from every matching Service. [source] Readiness probes run for the whole life of the container, so a Pod can go unready later too. [source]

A liveness probe is different: it decides when to restart a container. A startup probe runs only at startup and holds off the others until it succeeds. [source] Mixing them up is a classic mistake: a failing readiness probe never restarts anything.

Where it meets the Deployment: a Pod counts as ready via the probe, and available when it has been ready for minReadySeconds (default 0). The Deployment's progress is measured by new Pods becoming ready or available. [source] The docs list readiness probe failures among the causes of a Deployment getting stuck trying to deploy its newest ReplicaSet. [source]

The progressDeadlineSeconds field (default 600) is how long the controller waits before reporting that the rollout failed to progress. It surfaces as condition Progressing with status False and reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded. The controller keeps retrying; it does not roll back for you. If specified it must be greater than minReadySeconds. [source] Rolling back is a separate action you take. [source]

Probe fields and defaults (from the probe reference): initialDelaySeconds 0, periodSeconds 10, timeoutSeconds 1, successThreshold 1, failureThreshold 3. After failureThreshold failures in a row the container is not ready. For readiness the result counts as failed before the initial delay. [source] For HTTP probes, status codes from 200 up to but not including 400 count as success. [source]

Choosing settings: course decisions, not rules. The docs do not prescribe values for your app. A reasonable method for a simple web service: (1) point readiness at an endpoint that answers 200 only when this Pod can really serve requests; (2) pick periodSeconds small enough to notice problems (5 s is common) but not so small the probe is a load; (3) keep failureThreshold at 3 unless the endpoint is flaky; (4) use initialDelaySeconds or a startup probe so a slow start is not counted as failures; (5) set progressDeadlineSeconds comfortably above normal start time (plus minReadySeconds), so a healthy slow rollout is not reported as failed. Whether the readiness endpoint should check dependencies such as a database is a trade-off: the docs describe a readiness probe that additionally checks required backend services, which protects users from a Pod that cannot do its job but can make every Pod unready when a dependency blips. [source]

blocks.purpose: Show how a readiness probe sets the timeline from container start to receiving traffic, with the settings that control each interval.
blocks.alt: Timeline with four stages from left to right: container starts; initialDelaySeconds wait with no probes; probes every periodSeconds, failing, Pod not ready and receives no traffic; first success, Pod ready and added to Service endpoints; after minReadySeconds, Pod counts as available to the rollout. A note says the earliest time to unready after a failure is about failureThreshold times periodSeconds.

blocks.instructions: Decide, for each consequence, which probe it belongs to. Argue before you check: what happens to the Pod when this probe fails?
blocks.debrief: Readiness is about traffic (and therefore rollouts); liveness is about restarts; startup is about slow starts.

items.html: On repeated failure the kubelet restarts the container.
items.feedback: Liveness decides when to restart a container.

items.html: On failure the Pod is removed from the endpoints of matching Services.
items.feedback: Readiness controls whether the Pod receives Service traffic.

items.html: A new Pod that never passes it blocks a rolling update from finishing.
items.feedback: New Pods must become ready/available for the rollout to progress.

items.html: Runs only at startup, and holds off the other probes until it succeeds.
items.feedback: The startup probe gives a slow application time to initialise.

items.html: A deadlocked app that still holds its port open should be caught by this to recover.
items.feedback: Liveness catches a process that is running but cannot make progress.

items.html: Runs for the whole life of the container, and a Pod can become unready again later.
items.feedback: Readiness probes run during the container's whole lifecycle.

config.debrief: If you put a failing check in the wrong probe you either restart healthy Pods (liveness) or keep sending traffic to a broken Pod (no readiness).

blocks.title: Choosing settings for a simple web service

steps.html: Requirements (course scenario). A web API on port 8080 takes about 20 s to start, then answers GET /healthz with 200 only when its cache is loaded. Normal deploys must keep full capacity; a bad version should be detected within about 5 minutes.
A readiness probe: httpGet /healthz port 8080. The endpoint answers 200 only when the Pod can serve. This answers the question "should this Pod get traffic?" and gates the rollout.

Start takes ~20 s. initialDelaySeconds: 10, periodSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 3. Early failures before ~20 s are expected and harmless for readiness (the Pod is simply not ready yet). Later, a failing app turns unready after about 3 × 5 = 15 s. Course decision; not documented defaults.

steps.prompt: Pick the rollout parameters, remembering the limits from lesson 2.
steps.html:
strategy:
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 1
    maxUnavailable: 0
minReadySeconds: 10
progressDeadlineSeconds: 300

maxUnavailable 0 keeps capacity; maxSurge 1 gives the controller room to start one new Pod at a time. minReadySeconds: 10 means a Pod must stay ready 10 s before it is counted available. The deadline of 300 s is greater than minReadySeconds (required) and about 15 times the 20 s start time, so a healthy rollout is not reported failed but a stalled one is flagged in 5 minutes.

steps.prompt: Check: what happens if v2 returns 500 on /healthz forever?
steps.html: Pods never become ready, so the rollout stalls at ceiling 4 / floor 3 with 3 old Pods serving. After 300 s the Progressing condition reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded. The controller does not roll back; you roll back or fix.

blocks.result: Method: probe what "can serve" means, size the delays to the real start time, set the deadline a comfortable multiple above it, and re-run the stall check.

blocks.task:
This snippet has two problems for a service that takes ~30 s to start and must not lose capacity during deploys:

livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 5
strategy:
  rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 1 }
progressDeadlineSeconds: 20

Name the problems and write the corrected fragment.
hints: What happens to a container whose liveness probe fails before it finishes starting?
What does maxUnavailable 1 allow? Is the stall safe?
Is the deadline longer than the start time?
rubric: Liveness with short delay may restart a still-starting app; use a readiness probe/startup probe or a longer delay
maxUnavailable 1 allows capacity loss; use maxUnavailable 0 with maxSurge ≥ 1
Deadline 20 s is shorter than the 30 s start; raise it well above
blocks.solution: Problems: (1) only a liveness probe with a 5 s delay: it can restart the container while it is still starting, and nothing marks it ready/unready for traffic; (2) maxUnavailable: 1 with maxSurge: 0 lets capacity drop during a deploy; (3) the 20 s deadline is shorter than the 30 s start, so healthy rollouts would be reported as failed. Fix: add readinessProbe (httpGet /healthz, periodSeconds 5, failureThreshold 3), a startup probe or longer initial delay for any liveness probe, maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0, and progressDeadlineSeconds: 300.

blocks.task: Write a complete rollout configuration (readiness probe, strategy, minReadySeconds, progressDeadlineSeconds) for a web service with 6 replicas that starts in 45 s and whose /ready endpoint returns 200 only after warming a cache. Justify each number in one line and state the ceiling and floor. No hints.
rubric: Readiness probe httpGet /ready with sensible delays vs 45 s start
Ceiling and floor computed correctly from your chosen surge/unavailable
blocks.model: Example: readinessProbe httpGet /ready:8080, initialDelaySeconds 20, periodSeconds 5, failureThreshold 3; maxSurge 2 (ceiling 8), maxUnavailable 0 (floor 6); minReadySeconds 10; progressDeadlineSeconds 300 (> 45 + 10, with margin; must exceed minReadySeconds). Alternatives are valid: a startupProbe instead of initialDelay, or maxUnavailable 1 if brief capacity loss is acceptable. Numbers are course decisions, not documented requirements.

blocks.html: First attempts count as performance; later attempts are practice.

questions.prompt: A new Pod is Running, 0 restarts, but 0/1 ready, and the rollout is stuck. Which is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Running with 0/1 ready and no restarts points at readiness. A failing liveness probe would restart the container; an image pull error would prevent it from running.

feedback.0: Liveness failures cause restarts; there are none.
feedback.2: The container is running, so the image was pulled.

questions.prompt: What does the Deployment controller do when progressDeadlineSeconds expires on a stalled rollout?
options: Reports Progressing=False with reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded, and keeps retrying
questions.explanation: It reports the failure in the status condition and keeps retrying; rolling back is a separate action.

feedback.0: Automatic rollback is not done by the controller.
feedback.2: The new ReplicaSet is not deleted.

questions.prompt: Which setting pair is invalid according to the docs?
questions.explanation: The deadline, if specified, must be greater than minReadySeconds.

questions.prompt: In your own words: why does a failing readiness probe stall a rolling update but not cause an outage when maxUnavailable is 0?
rubric: New Pods not ready never count as available
The controller can create no more new Pods (surge) and cannot remove old ones
questions.model: New Pods stay not ready, so the available count stays at the floor and the surge ceiling is used up; the controller has no legal move. The old Pods remain ready and serve traffic, so there is no outage, only a stalled rollout that reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded after the deadline.

blocks.task: New context: an internal reporting service has 2 replicas. Its start-up loads a 90-second report cache. The team sets readinessProbe: httpGet /healthz, periodSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 3 and leaves everything else default. Their deploys now often end with ProgressDeadlineExceeded even though the app eventually works. Explain why, with numbers, and propose two changes with their trade-offs. Do not run anything.
rubric: Notes default progressDeadlineSeconds 600 so this alone would not fail at 90 s start; identifies the plausible cause as readiness never succeeding or the probe/endpoint not matching real readiness, OR flags that more information is needed
Computes the surge/unavailable limits for 2 replicas (ceiling 3, floor 2)
Proposes a startup probe or initialDelay and/or an adequate deadline
blocks.model: With defaults (progressDeadlineSeconds 600), a 90 s start should not by itself exceed the deadline, so the course reasoning: either /healthz returns non-200 for longer than 600 s (a real bug, or it waits on something slow) or the endpoint does not reflect readiness. Limits: ceiling 3, floor 2, one new Pod at a time, so a 90 s start per Pod means roughly 2 × 90 s of serial rollout, still within 600 s. Changes: (1) use a startupProbe or initialDelaySeconds so early failures are not misread (trade-off: slower detection of an immediately broken version); (2) make /healthz return 200 only when the cache is loaded and test it, or set progressDeadlineSeconds higher (trade-off: slower failure reporting). The point is the method; exact figures are course reasoning.

blocks.prompt: Explain in your own words how a readiness probe, maxUnavailable and progressDeadlineSeconds together determine whether a bad version causes an outage, a stall, or a reported failure.
